part_title: Analytics, EC2, Chat Operations and Glue Assistance
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 11 through 14 individually in source order, verifying visible labels, workflows, examples, access-control boundaries, and service distinctions; rewritten as balanced-length teaching narration.

scenes.title: Generative BI in Amazon Quick
scenes.narration: This slide demonstrates generative business intelligence in Amazon Quick Sight, with the natural-language experience shown as part of Amazon Quick. An analyst asks, 'What are the sales by region?' The assistant interprets the question against an existing Quick Sight dataset rather than inventing sales values. The middle of the diagram shows the data source, including tables and fields, leading to a generated bar chart and executive summary. The illustrative chart compares North America, EMEA, APAC and LATAM. Since no actual values are supplied here, treat the heights as an example of the presentation, not as audited sales figures. Follow the lower walkthrough: ask the question, identify the relevant dataset fields, generate the visual, then review and refine the analysis. A business analyst still needs to check filters, date ranges, definitions and totals before sharing a conclusion. The exam distinction is that natural-language BI helps users create and explore visualizations without writing all the queries or charts from scratch. It does not eliminate the need for trustworthy datasets and human validation.

scenes.title: EC2 instance type guidance
scenes.narration: Here Q Developer helps narrow down suitable EC2 instance families for a new workload. Start with requirements on the left: the example needs sixteen virtual CPUs and one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes of RAM for memory-heavy data processing. A virtual CPU represents a unit of compute capacity; RAM holds working data while the application runs. Q Developer considers candidate families rather than making an irreversible selection. The three colored options distinguish compute-optimized instances for CPU-intensive tasks, memory-optimized instances for larger working memory, and storage-optimized instances for demanding local storage throughput. Given the example's large RAM requirement, memory-optimized is a logical family to investigate first. The human evaluation panel is essential: check current regional pricing, Availability Zone availability, networking, storage and application constraints before deployment. The bottom-right contrast is also exam-relevant. Choosing an instance for a new workload is different from AWS Compute Optimizer rightsizing an existing fleet using observed utilization. A recommendation is a starting point for evidence-based sizing, not a guarantee of the best instance.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer in chat applications
scenes.narration: This slide traces an operational alert into a team's chat channel. On the left, Amazon CloudWatch detects that CPU utilization is high and an alarm enters the ALARM state. Amazon SNS is the notification service that delivers the alarm to the configured integration. The Q Developer chat application, formerly associated with AWS Chatbot, can then provide guidance in Slack or Microsoft Teams within the permissions granted to it. Look at the example on the right: HighCPUUtilization is in ALARM for an EC2 instance. Q Developer suggests checking the current CloudWatch CPU metrics, identifying processes consuming CPU, reviewing recent deployments and considering scaling if the load is expected. The bottom sequence shows the developer asking for help in the same Slack channel and receiving diagnostic next steps. This saves context switching during an incident, but it does not automatically remediate the issue. The team must verify the alarm, assess user impact, investigate likely causes and approve operational changes. Remember the distinction: CloudWatch detects, SNS delivers, the assistant explains, and authorized people or automation perform the fix.

scenes.title: Amazon Q data integration in AWS Glue
scenes.narration: This slide connects natural-language data preparation to AWS Glue. Start at the top left: an engineer asks to read order records from Amazon S3, remove rows with null values in key fields, select required columns, and write a curated dataset. Amazon Q data integration suggests a Glue extract-transform-load script. ETL means extracting data, transforming it into the needed structure, and loading the cleaned results. Before execution, the engineer reviews the proposed transformations, checks the input schema and IAM permissions, and validates what 'null' should mean for the business. Then a Glue job runs and writes curated order data back into S3. The lower left example shows the key fields: order ID, customer ID, order date and amount. On the right is a troubleshooting path for a failed Glue job. Read the job logs and stack trace, use the assistant to interpret likely data-quality, schema or permission problems, then investigate and correct the script before rerunning. The assistant proposes a plan; the engineer remains responsible for validating it and confirming the output is complete and accurate.
